decks.name: LeetCode #150 - Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
decks.description: Evaluate the value of an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation

cards.question: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation: You are given an array of strings tokens that represents an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation. Evaluate the expression and return an integer that represents the value of the expression. Valid operators are '+', '-', '*', and '/'. Each operand may be an integer or another expression. Note that division between two integers should truncate toward zero. It is guaranteed that the given RPN expression is always valid.

solutions.name: Stack
solutions.explanation: Use a stack to process tokens from left to right. For numbers, push them onto the stack. For operators, pop two operands, perform the operation, and push the result back. The final result is the only element remaining in the stack. This is the standard and most efficient approach for evaluating RPN expressions.

solutions.name: Recursion
solutions.explanation: Process tokens from right to left using recursion. Start from the last token and recursively evaluate the expression. When we encounter an operator, recursively evaluate the right operand first, then the left operand, then apply the operator. This works because RPN is naturally suited for recursive evaluation from right to left.

solutions.name: Doubly Linked List
solutions.explanation: Build a doubly linked list from the tokens, then traverse it to find operators. When an operator is found, compute the result using the two previous nodes, update the operator node's value to the result, and remove the two operand nodes by adjusting pointers. Continue until traversal completes. Less efficient than stack but demonstrates linked list manipulation.

solutions.name: Brute Force
solutions.explanation: Repeatedly scan through the tokens array to find the first operator. When found, compute the result using the two preceding operands, create a new array with the result replacing those three elements, and repeat until only one element remains. Inefficient due to repeated array operations and scans.
